Recursively partition the envelope:\n   - At each node: split into two sub-rectangles.\n   - Assign each room to one side based on area-balanced bipartition.\n   - Recurse on each side.\n   - Leaf: a single room placed in its sub-rectangle, top-left aligned.\n\n4. Backtrack on infeasibility:\n   - If a leaf can't fit (sub-rectangle smaller than room dims):\n     return None to the parent.\n   - Parent tries alternative cut positions in canonical order\n     (cut fraction varies in 0.1 increments from balanced toward\n     extremes).\n   - If all alternatives exhausted: bubble up the backtrack.\n\n5. Worst case: O(n!) per the spec acknowledgment. For typical n \u2264 15\n   the heuristic is fast (O(n log n) expected).\n\nThe implementation is INTENTIONALLY iteration-deterministic:\nevery choice point uses a fixed canonical order. This guarantees\nInv 7 byte-equal replay across runs given identical inputs +\nconfiguration.\n\"\"\"\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nfrom typing import Literal\n\nfrom ..bounds import DEFAULT_GRID_SNAP_M, snap_to_grid\nfrom ..errors import GeometricInfeasibilityError\nfrom ..schema import PlacedRoom\nfrom .room_spec import RoomSpec\n\n\n# Bisection axis choices in their CANONICAL TRY ORDER (per v0.2-A4\n# rule #6): always try vertical (x-axis cut) first, then horizontal\n# (y-axis cut) on backtrack. We assign each room to\n    the side whose current area is furthest below its target.\n\n    Determinism: same input order \u2192 same output partition.\n    \"\"\"\n    if not rooms:\n        return ((), ())\n\n    total_area = sum(r.area_m2 for r in rooms)\n    target_a_area = total_area * target_fraction\n\n    side_a: list[RoomSpec] = []\n    side_b: list[RoomSpec] = []\n    a_area = 0.0\n    b_area = 0.0\n\n    for room in rooms:\n        # Choose the side whose current area is furthest below its\n        # target.       "file_text": "\"\"\"\nBuildemUp \u2014 Component 12 \u2014 Multi-Floor Refinement Absorption (MFRA)\n=====================================================================\n\nPer C12 SPEC v1.0 LOCKED v0.2-A2 (formal MFRA convergence) + v0.2-A10\n(vertical-core reservation pre-step).\n\nAlgorithm (\u00a7 3 Phase 2 step 4):\n\n1. Initial pass:\n   a. Run Phase 1b: reserve vertical cores at the SAME (x, y) on\n      every floor (prevents iteration oscillation).\n   b. Run Phase 1 SFP per floor (slicing-tree).\n   c. Run Phase 2 step 3 VAV across floors.\n   d. If converged: emit MultiFloorPlacedCandidate.\n\n2. Retry loop (bounded by multi_floor_max_realign_iterations,\n   default 3 per v0.3-A2):\n   a. For each misaligned feature f:\n      - Identify the floor F whose centroid deviates most from\n        consensus.\n      - Inject a HARD position constraint into F's SFP retry:\n        f.target_position = mean(positions across non-deviant floors)\n        with \u03b5-tolerance = (alignment_tolerance / 2).\n      - Re-run SFP on F with the constraint added.\n   b. Re-run VAV.\n   c. Convergence criterion (monotonic-\u03b4):\n      - If \u03b4_{n+1} < \u03b4_n \u00d7 0.5: continue (good progress)\n      - If \u03b4_n \u00d7 0.5 \u2264 \u03b4_{n+1} < \u03b4_n: continue (slow progress)\n      - If \u03b4_{n+1} \u2265 \u03b4_n: ABORT (divergence/plateau)\n   d. If retries exhausted without convergence: raise\n      VerticalAlignmentError.\n\nFor v1, the constraint-injection step (2a) is implemented as a\nsimple \"biased re-placement\": we don't currently re-run the full\nslicing-tree with hard constraints (that's a deeper integration\nfiled as B-C12-COUPLED-MF-PLACEMENT). v1 instead does best-effort:\nif the initial VAV fails, MFRA reports the convergence outcome\nhonestly without pretending to fix it via single-pass retry.         "text": "A classical discrete formulation casts layout as a quadratic assignment problem (QAP): assign n facilities to n locations to minimize the flow-distance cost with a permutation constraint on assignments (Koopmans and Beckmann, 1957; Loiola et al., 2007; QAPLIB). Even this stylized model is NP-hard and remains challenging as n grows.\n\nThis study targets discrete, grid-based layouts with logic-heavy constraints that arise in practice: one-to-one assignment of machines to slots, adjacency requirements (must be neighbors), separation constraints (forbidden neighbors), aisles or unavailable cells, and optional multi-floor slotting. These constraints generate dense combinatorial structure on top of assignment. \n\nWhile mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is strong for structured formulations and linearizable objectives, and CP-SAT excels at rich Boolean logic with pseudo-Boolean/linear reasoning, modern CDCL-style SAT solvers offer a complementary capability: rapid conflict-driven pruning of large combinatorial spaces. CDCL learns clauses (\"nogoods\") from conflicts and, with VSIDS branching, prioritizes variables that explain recent conflicts (Marques-Silva and Sakallah, 1999; Moskewicz et al., 2001; Biere et al., 2021). CDCL/MaxSAT methods have delivered strong\n\nresults in adjacent layout-like domains such as EDA placement/routing and orthogonal packing (Soh et al., 2008; Grandcolas and Pinto, 2010; Cohen, Nadel, and Ryvchin, 2021).\n\nDespite this success, plain CNF/CDCL SAT has rarely been applied to full-scale factory FLP.\n\n\n\nLikely reasons include an optimization-feasibility mismatch (SAT is a decision framework; FLP is an optimization task), the clause overhead of encoding arithmetic and cardinality constraints, and the ready availability of CP-SAT and MILP tooling for FLP variants (Biere et al., 2021; Bailleux and Boufkhad, 2003; Sinz, 2005). Rather than \u2026\n\nCP-SAT uses lazy clause generation to combine constraint propagation with SAT solving. Here\u2019s how it works: Propagation first: When a variable is assigned, constraint propagation runs to completion, eliminating infeasible values from domains. Detect conflicts: If propagation detects infeasibility (a domain becomes empty), analyze the conflict. Generate clauses: The conflict analysis produces a learned clause explaining why the conflict occurred. This clause is expressed in SAT form (a disjunction of Boolean literals). \n\nThe specialized AllDifferent propagator uses matching algorithms from graph theory. It can detect infeasibility much earlier and propagate more effectively. For example, if you have 5 variables, 4 of which already have domain {1, 2}, AllDifferent immediately detects infeasibility (4 variables competing for 2 values).\n\nConstraint propagation: Core technique using specialized propagators for different constraint types. Lazy clause generation: Translates constraint programming into SAT and uses CDCL. Linear programming relaxations: For certain constraints (particularly arithmetic constraints over large domains), CP-SAT uses LP relaxations to compute bounds and prune domains. Large neighborhood search: A local search technique that finds and improves solutions by fixing some variables and re-optimizing others. This is effective at finding good solutions quickly.",
